q: Calculate D for each plot.
Both plots have the same species and the same number of trees. Explain why D differs.
Evenness: plot B is dominated by oak (75% of trees), while plot A has the species in similar numbers.
An oak disease arrives. Predict which plot loses more of its trees, and explain.
Plot B: three-quarters of its trees are oaks, against 30% in plot A.
Explain why plot A is likely to support more animal species.
A more even mix of trees gives a wider variety of food and habitats (niches).
State one limitation of comparing just these two plots.
One plot of each may not be representative; repeats are needed.
Rank the five species by EDGE score.
Pangolin, olm, aye-aye, tiger, house sparrow.
Explain why the olm scores highly, although it is only vulnerable.
It is very evolutionarily distinct: 45 million years of unique history with few close relatives, so its loss would remove a lot of evolutionary history.
Explain why the tiger scores lower than the aye-aye, although both are endangered.
The tiger has close relatives (other big cats), so its ED is low; the aye-aye has no close relatives.
Give one argument for spending conservation money on tigers anyway.
Tigers are a flagship and umbrella species: protecting their large habitat protects many other species, and they attract public support and funding.
Suggest one limitation of the EDGE method.
Any one: it ignores a species’ ecological role (keystone species); ED values are estimates; it ignores the cost or chance of success.
